Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) developed in a 60-year-old
woman. Treatment with diazepam controlled her painful
spasms initially. Two and one-half years after the onset of
SMS, she developed new spells of paroxysmal leg jerking
and apnea. A spell was recorded with simultaneous video and
polygraphic techniques that revealed simultaneous firing of
motor unit potentials in several muscles (paraspinals, internal
hamstring, and abdominal muscles). Apnea was associated
with arterial oxygen desaturation. An increase in the dose of
diazepam decreased the number and severity of these latter
episodes. Seventeen months later, the patient began to taper
the diazepam. Shortly thereafter, she suffered a cardiorespira-
tory arrest and subsequently died. Autopsy showed small
chronic inflammatory foci in the pancreas (some associated
with islets) and findings of diffuse encephalomyelitis charac-
terized by perivascular cuffing in the spinal cord, brainstem,
thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala, and a dense mononu-
clear infiltrate in the anterior horns of the lumbar and cervical
cord with relative preservation of axons and myelin. Cell
typing showed this infiltrate to be polyclonal and reactive.
There have been rare cases of SMS associated with encepha-
lomyelitis reported previously. We conclude that our patient
is an example of coexistence of these 2 conditions.
